item.title: The Slingshot: No roof and no plan
item.description: The Slingshot: No roof and no plan
item.content:encoded:
There were no rental cars left.

My brother Kyle and I flew out for a wedding in Colorado, went to grab our car, and there was nothing. Sold out. So we got on Turo and took the only thing available, which turned out to be a Slingshot -- basically a roofless go-kart. Then we drove it about four hours into the mountains.

No roof, no windshield, no real plan. Just the two of us, a borrowed go-kart, and a lot of wind. Like a lot. It was stupid and kind of uncomfortable and one of the better drives I've had in a while.

I've told this story before and laughed about it plenty of times since. But it stuck with me more than I expected, and I think it's because of the sideways part. The trip we planned would've been fine, but the one we got is the one I'll remember.

Things go sideways, and that’s the part you actually remember.

When the plan falls through

Every business I've worked in runs into the sold-out-rental-counter moment. The launch slips or the new hire doesn't work out. The thing you were so sure of turns out to be dead wrong. It happens, and the whole game is what you do in the next five minutes -- reach for the keys and drive, or stand at the counter.

I'm not naturally good at this.

My instinct is to freak out. But what's changed over the years is that I've got a little more practice driving the proverbial go-kart, and I've watched enough detours transform into the good parts to trust it a bit more each time.

Why the boring reps matter

I've been in the gym a lot lately. Nothing dramatic, just showing up most days and picking up something heavy and putting it down. It's the least interesting hour of my day. But I think the reps you put in when nothing's happening are what you draw on when everything comes to a head.

That's true of a gym, and it's true of a business. The teams that handle a crisis well aren't lucky. They did the boring work -- wrote things down, built the systems, tracked what mattered -- back when nothing was on fire. So when the car rental comes up empty, they had something to reach for.

Half the people I work with live in this world too, funny enough. Founders building something special, coaches who spend a decade getting good at a thing, leaders getting their IP down on paper.

People who trust that the reps add up even when the day doesn't feel like progress.

One thing to sit with this week

Think about the last thing that went sideways on you, and how you took it. The calm to enjoy a detour usually isn't about the detour. It's those reps from earlier, in the boring stretch when nothing was going wrong.

So put in the boring reps. They're what let you enjoy the sideways parts when they show up.

Shane

item.title: Why does the biz only work when you're in the room?
item.description: Why does the biz only work when you're in the room?
item.content:encoded:
Three years ago, a playground and I had a disagreement. The playground won.

We were halfway through an eight-hour drive to the Outer Banks, stopped for dinner, letting the girls run around. Next thing I knew, I was in an ER getting a brace, then spent the whole beach week on crutches while poor Skyler hauled the chairs, the coolers, the umbrellas, a three-year-old, an eight-month-old, and me back and forth across the sand every day.

Not my finest trip. But being stuck like that got me thinking about something I see in a lot of the businesses I work with. Went back through a few things I wrote this past month and noticed all three were really pointing toward the same idea.

Most of the valuable stuff inside a small business lives in one person's head. That's what makes it valuable, but it's also what makes it fragile.

When the room empties

A lot of the groups I work with only run well when one specific person is there. They're the individual, usually the founder, who knows how it all fits together. So the day they step out, traveling (or sick or laid up on crutches at a beach house), the whole thing idles until they're back.

It works despite those pauses for a while. But it's a nervous way to run, and most founders can feel it's a matter of time before a pause lands somewhere it can't afford to.

A question worth sitting with: If you couldn't show up for two weeks, no phone, no laptop, what would stop moving? Not slow down. Stop. That list is the map. Every item on it is a place where the business is really just you.

Getting it out of your head

So how do you actually do that? A client from this past year comes to mind.

They're a golf fitness brand, built over a decade. A serious operation -- 600+ videos, hundreds of workouts, a big engaged audience, real revenue. The method that made it work was genuinely good. It just lived mostly in the founder's head and scattered across a library nobody could fully see.

We got it out, and the process was less mysterious than it sounds. We indexed everything they already had. Then a standing weekly call where I'd ask questions and let him talk, and we'd get the method down on paper, tagged, and organized into a knowledge base.

It doesn't sound fancy. Just an hour where the goal was to move what he knew from his head into a place other people could reach.

Nobody writes a manual on their own time. But most people will happily answer questions about the thing they're best at.

That's the trick. You talk, someone else captures. Once it reached critical mass, we could shape it into a certification with course modules, all drawing from that one source.

If I were starting this in your business, I'd start with the messiest thing that only you can do. Extract that piece from your head, build the process, and move onto the next.

Why it's worth the trouble

Here's the part that ties it together, and it comes from a mentor of mine, Ken.

The best sales advice he ever gave me was to stop selling. He gets on a call and doesn't pitch or talk price. He digs into your problem until he understands it, and starts helping right there. His logic is that he wants to be sure he can add real value before he asks for anything. By the time cost comes up, the trust is already built.

I've been trying to run more like that. Get in, look around, be useful first, tell you the truth about what I see, even when the truth is "you don't need me for this."

And here's the connection I didn't see until I lined these up. When everything's trapped in your head, you're rationing yourself. When it's out where you can hand pieces of it over, being generous gets easy. Getting the knowledge out of your head is what makes being useful-first even possible.

item.title: Early recognition is often borrowed (and that's okay)
item.description: Practical ways to borrow trust for your certification early.
item.content:encoded:
One of the quiet misunderstandings I see over and over again is this:

Organizations assume that if they design a certification well enough, the market will simply recognize it.

But that’s rarely how it works.

Most respected credentials didn’t start with organic trust. They borrowed it. It wasn't in a deceptive way or through hype - it was through alignment. 

Where early recognition actually comes from

If you trace almost any credible certification back to its early days, you’ll usually find one (or more) of these conditions:

→ Alignment with a known institution

→ Partnership with a respected brand

→ Adoption by a small group of influential early users

In other words, the credential didn’t prove itself alone. It was introduced into the market through existing trust networks.

Many teams delay action while waiting for recognition to magically appear, but that delay often costs more credibility than moving forward strategically.

Borrowed trust vs. manufactured hype

There’s an important distinction here.

Borrowed trust looks like partnering with organizations that already serve your audience and being embedded in real workflows or hiring decisions, so others validate your standard before you promote it.

On the other hand, manufactured hype looks like over-polished branding with no external signal, big launches without ecosystem buy-in, and claiming authority before anyone else does.

Borrowed trust isn’t a shortcut around rigor. If anything, it usually forces it earlier.

External visibility makes weak standards obvious, but that pressure is a feature, not a bug.

Practical ways to borrow trust early

Here are a few ways we see organizations do this well:

1. Anchor to a real-world use case

Instead of launching broadly, start where the credential clearly solves a problem:

  • Hiring
  • Compliance
  • Partner enablement
  • Client delivery

Recognition grows faster when the credential does something specific.

2. Partner before you promote

Look for associations, platforms, employers, and networks that already convene your ideal practitioners. It's better to have a quiet pilot with them as the right partner than a loud solo launch. 

3. Let early adopters be visible

Your first certified cohort matters disproportionately. 

Highlight:

  • Where they work
  • How they use the credential
  • Why they sought it out

Recognition spreads laterally, not top-down.

4. Design for reference, not persuasion

Early on, your goal isn’t to convince everyone. It’s to make it easy for others to say:

“This is the credential we look for.”

That changes what you emphasize:

  • Standards over stories
  • Clarity over cleverness
  • Proof over polish
  • The long game

Over time, borrowed trust becomes earned trust.

The partnerships fade into the background, the standard stands on its own, and the credential starts showing up unprompted in bios, job listings, and RFPs.

But that only happens if you’re willing to engage the ecosystem early - not wait for recognition to arrive fully formed.

→ If you’re building (or refining) a certification, I'm curious: Whose trust could you responsibly borrow first?

Onward,

– Shane

item.title: The Certification Readiness Test: 10 Questions to Know If Your IP Can Carry a Credential
item.description: Before you build anything, answer these 10 questions.
item.content:encoded:
When people come to us thinking about turning their work into a certification, we don’t start with platforms or badges.

We start with fit.

Because the biggest trap I see is when someone thinks a certification is just a fancier course. It’s not. A certification is proof that you finished something, a public standard, and a longer-term initiative that often includes renewals and community.

Over the years, we’ve identified 10 major questions that predict whether a certification is likely to work for your business (and whether the investment makes sense).

So before you build anything, here’s the readiness test we use:

The 10-question readiness test

Usually, we look at four buckets:

  1. IP
  2. Demand
  3. Business-model fit
  4. Brand readiness

And in practice, you can use the following 10 questions to determine where you currently are on the readiness scale.

1️⃣ Do you have a repeatable IP?
Is your “method” something you can teach through a course, workshop, book, or process, so it can be applied consistently?

2️⃣ Is there a clear market demand for what you do?
Not “it’s interesting,” but a clear pull for the product or service your IP supports.

3️⃣ Are clients asking for higher levels of training? 
A signal that the market wants “deeper mastery,” not just an intro.

4️⃣ Do you have an audience list? 
Because a credential needs a reachable, committed people to launch to.

5️⃣ Do you have a social following?
Same idea: do you have an existing channel where people already pay attention?

6️⃣ Does your work have enough recognition that people would want to associate with it?
In other words, does affiliating with your brand feel valuable to your audience?

7️⃣ Do you actually want to introduce this into your business stack? 
A certification isn’t just a content project - it becomes part of how your business operates.

8️⃣ Does scalable recurring revenue make sense for your model?
Versus relying mostly on one-off course sales or one-on-one work.

9️⃣ Is your brand strong enough to diffuse through other people?
Meaning, are you ready for other individuals and groups to represent your brand moving forward by getting your certification?

🔟 Are you ready to introduce that into the mix?
Brand diffusion changes everything - support, governance, consistency, expectations. Are you ready for that responsibility?

A simple way to interpret your score

If you’re strong on IP + demand, you can build something.

If you’re strong on brand + audience, you can probably launch something.

But if you’re not ready for renewals + community + ongoing engagement, what you’re building may behave more like a course than a certification - and the market will treat it that way.

👉 If you answered “yes” to most of these but hesitated on one, which question is the bottleneck for you right now?

Reply and let me know.

Keep up the good work,

– Shane

item.title: From Course to Credential: What We're Learning About Go-to-Market Strategy
item.description: The work didn't change. The positioning did.
item.content:encoded:
A few weeks ago, I was speaking with someone who has taught hundreds of people how to build online courses. And she said something that’s stuck with me:

“They keep coming back, asking what to do next. I don’t know what to tell them.”

For many of her clients, the initial success is there. They’ve built a course, delivered it to a few cohorts, and maybe even made it profitable.

But eventually, the question shows up: 
What now?

The next step isn’t always obvious

Some try to launch another course. Others explore books, cohorts, or masterminds.

But what this educator kept hearing (and feeling herself) was a desire to solidify what they’d built:

→ To give their method a little more structure.
→ A little more recognition.
→ A little more staying power.

And for a long time, she had the same instinct I did:

“Maybe what they need isn't something new, but a clear next step.”

Building the product before the pitch

At some point, I realized I wasn’t just helping her shape what came next - I was relearning something about my own work.

It reminded me of something I’d forgotten:

It’s easy to get stuck polishing the idea in your own head.
Harder, but more valuable, to refine it in dialogue with your customers.

That’s what’s been happening. And that’s what started to reshape how I think about our own go-to-market.

Rethinking the GTM stack

Historically, we’d lead with services: brand, website, content, campaigns. But the more we talked to people interested in exploring a "next step" in their business, the more we realized:

They weren’t asking for a website.

They were asking for direction:

→ “How do I structure this?”
→ “How does this fit into what I’ve already built?”
→ “How does this become a new revenue stream for my business?”

The work didn't change, but what we led with did.

This is why we built a playbook, not just for delivery, but for go-to-market.

We’d help define the certification itself, but also offer the services for:

  • Messaging and positioning
  • Website and landing page copy
  • Launch plan
  • Optional paid ad strategy (if they’re ready)

All of this has been offered upfront, not as marketing for their business, but as a new business line in itself.

And that’s created a very different kind of conversation.

When the positioning finally clicked

We didn't reinvent what we do, but we did get clearer on what people were actually buying.

And as a founder, I’ve been re-learning something I thought I already knew:

People don’t really want marketing.
They want forward motion.

Most go-to-market strategies assume that the customer already knows what they want next.

In reality, many of the people you’re talking to don’t, and that's not a failure - it's a natural consequence of success.

So when your customer is asking:

“What is the most sensible next move, given what I’ve already built?”

... your GTM has to answer that.

At the end of the day, this isn't just about certifications. It's about what happens when you give people structure for:

  • Their ideas
  • Their IP
  • Their revenue and go-to market strategy

That’s why this model is starting to click.

You won't only be selling another service.

You'll be giving people a next step that makes sense for them and aligns with what their audience is already asking for.

→ What is the big "next step" that you're planning for 2026? I'd love to hear what's currently on your mind.

Onward into 2026,

– Shane

item.title: What Taylor Swift taught me about certifications
item.description: My wife's a Swiftie. The loyalty structure isn't that different from what we're building.
item.content:encoded:
My wife is a massive Taylor Swift fan.

We've traveled to Portugal, Toronto, Miami, and Indianapolis. Watching her engage with that community has been great, honestly, and I've been thinking about why the Taylor Swift phenomenon works so well as a business.

There are some uncomfortable parallels to certification that I can't ignore.

Stay with me here:

What Taylor and certifications both do: they create identity alignment.

When my wife identifies as a Swiftie, she's aligning herself with values: authenticity, storytelling, resilience, and community. The music is the vehicle, but the identity is what creates loyalty.

Certification works the same way. When someone becomes certified in your methodology, they're aligning their professional identity with it.

They're publicly stating: "This is how I do my work. This is what I believe in."

That alignment creates loyalty that course completion never could.

Parallel #1. The recurring revenue structure

🎵 Taylor has: concerts, albums, re-releases, merch drops, and vault tracks.
🎯 Certifications have: applications, exams, continuing ed, renewals, and events.

Both models create ongoing participation. Swifties stay engaged. Same with credential holders; they're invested in maintaining their standing over time.

Parallel #2. The community component

Swifties have their bracelet exchanges, concert meetups, and online groups. There's shared language and inside jokes.

It's tribal, and it creates belonging.

Certifications do this through cohorts, directories, annual events, and community forums. Credential holders identify with each other. They reference shared training experiences and help each other navigate the standard.

The tribe forms naturally because everyone's invested in the same system.

Parallel #3. Markers of allegiance

Taylor has these clear signals of participation: the number of concerts you’ve been to, whether you have the vinyls, and whether you have the limited edition.

There are levels showing how invested you are.

Certifications have similar markers of allegiance:
→ Which version of the standard did you train under?
→ Have you recertified?
→ Are you in the directory?
→ Do you have an advanced credential?

Each marker signals depth of commitment.

Parallel #4. The expansion

Taylor started in country, moved to pop, went into filmmaking, and influenced fashion. The brand expands into adjacent spaces while keeping the core identity intact. Swifties follow because they trust her instincts and want to be part of whatever's next.

Certifications evolve similarly.

The core methodology stays consistent, but you add advanced credentials, specialized applications, and partnerships.

The ecosystem expands around the original standard. Practitioners follow because they're already invested and trust where you're taking it.

I'm not suggesting certifications need to become fandoms. The loyalty mechanics are worth studying, though.

When you build a system that:

  • Lets people align their identity with your work
  • Gives them recurring reasons to participate
  • Creates community around shared values
  • Offers clear markers of belonging

...you are inviting them into a long-term relationship.

That's what creates lasting authority: a structure people want to belong to.

DRVN Golf is seeing this unfold with their network. Their trainers identify with the methodology rather than simply using it, putting it on their websites and referencing it throughout their client conversations.

They want to be known as "the trainer who uses the DRVN system."

Taylor Swift is running a certification model. (She probably doesn't think about it that way, but the structure is there.)

And if it works for building one of the most loyal fan bases in the world, maybe there's something here worth learning from.

→ Have you seen any brands or methodologies that create this kind of loyalty in your space?

P.S. This one's for my wife. I "get it" now.


– Shane

item.title: Your website is a product, not a poster
item.description: Certification websites need to think about what they do, not how they look.
item.content:encoded:
Many certification organizations I meet treat their sites like a poster.

They are places to announce or describe what they do. It looks good, but serves little purpose.

Yet in 2025, most people have their first and most meaningful interaction with your program through the website. It’s where they apply, find standards and templates, confirm credentials, and return to stay engaged.

The website has become the product itself:

→ It is measurable. Products have metrics. You can track how many users complete an application, where they drop off, and which resources are most used. When you have this data, you can make improvements for better results.

→ It is iterative. Products evolve. Your standards and your systems change, so your site should as well. The most successful organizations don’t redesign every five years; they make small, regular improvements each quarter.

→ It is integrated. Your website should connect to your CRM, certification portal, and community systems. When those pieces work together, your team stops repeating work and starts learning from its data because it can see how visitors travel from the first visit to working with you.

When you shift to looking at your website as a product, you can focus on its goal.

The strongest certification organizations are quietly building trust infrastructure: digital systems that reflect the credibility of their brand through how usable and connected they are.

They don’t have inexplicable drop-offs between applications and submissions - they know what happened to the users, and how they can make it better in the next iteration cycle.

So when a website doesn’t deliver, it’s not a lack of effort. In most cases, it simply means it reflects an old set of goals or plays by old rules.

Once the purpose is clear, the design naturally finds its direction. And when digital is treated as a product, it becomes an investment in the mission itself rather than just the promotion of pretty words.

→ If you had to pick one thing your website should do better today, what would it be?

Onward,
Shane

item.title: You're Not Starting From Zero: The 70% Rule for Certification
item.description: Your existing IP is worth more than you realize. Here's how to make it certification-ready.
item.content:encoded:
Over the last several months, I’ve been having a version of the same conversation.

The question I keep getting: "Am I ready to build a certification?"

The answer I keep giving: "You've probably been ready for a while."

There's this persistent myth that certifications are ivory tower territory. That you need to be LEED or some massive accreditation body to create a legitimate credential. That the barrier to entry is prohibitively high.

But there is a really unique and powerful opportunity for businesses to leverage existing IP to create certifications.

If you’ve written a book, built a course, taught workshops, or documented your process for clients, you’ve already done the hard part. That’s your IP. And it’s usually 70–80% of what a certification requires.

When we work with leaders, the first thing we do is audit what already exists. Books. Slides. Course modules. Case studies. Frameworks. We line them up against what certification needs:

  • A standard (what good looks like)
  • Education content (teaching to that standard)
  • Assessment (verifying competency)

Most of the time, the standard is already embedded in your work. The education is 70% there. What’s left is packaging: pricing, positioning, brand, and renewal.

We recently had a conversation with a super neat golf fitness company. They already had a training app and a clear methodology, but they needed some support in formalizing their existing work into a certification that would attract members, build credibility, and ultimately grow their business. 

All we did was:

  • Formalize their method into a standard
  • Reorganize their videos into education modules
  • Build pricing and branding around the credential

If you’ve built IP that delivers results, you’re closer to certification than you realize.

👉 What IP have you already built that might be 70% of the way there?

Reply and let me know if I can help.

Onward,
Shane

item.title: Want to build a certification that actually matters?
item.description: Anyone can slap a badge on a site. But trust? That takes more.
item.content:encoded:
Anyone can slap a badge on a website.

But real certification? That’s about trust. And trust is earned.

In every project I’ve worked on, from LEED to WELL to the new programs we’re helping launch today, the same four credibility levers always show up.

Here are the four credibility levers:

1️⃣ A Clear, Public Standard
No gatekeeping. No mystery. Just visible, auditable expectations.

2️⃣ Transparent Requirements
So anyone (not just insiders) can understand what it takes to pass.

3️⃣ Ongoing Evaluation
Certification shouldn’t be one-and-done. It has to evolve with science, new information, or evolving priorities.

4️⃣ Market Recognition
If no one asks for it, it won’t last. The market has to care.

That’s what separates a certification from a course. It’s what moves it from content… to currency.

If you’re building a certification, these four pillars should show up in every slide deck, every system, every strategy.

I once helped lead a standard that scaled to 100+ countries, and it started by getting these four things right.

So let me ask: 👉 What do you think your market values most in a credential?

Reply and let me know.

Onward,
Shane

item.title: When "good enough" websites cost you more than you think
item.description: When your site isn't built to grow with you, it's quietly holding you back.
item.content:encoded:
In the certification world, here’s something I see all too often: A site launches. It looks good, and everyone breathes a sigh of relief.

And then… six months later, the cracks start to show. 

Why the Cracks Appear

Maybe it’s an integration that never quite works the way it should. Or a lead form that collects contacts but never syncs with the CRM. Maybe the content structure is so rigid that even small updates feel like open-heart surgery. Or the team slowly realizes that the site was never actually built to support their growth strategy in the first place.

That’s the hidden cost of “good enough.”

The best websites in our space are more than pretty.

 ✔️ Purpose-built for your audiences and user journeys

 ✔️ Connected to your systems so data flows, not clogs

 ✔️ Flexible enough to adapt as your programs evolve

 ✔️ Measured so you know what’s working and what’s not

When your website works like a brochure, you’re forcing your team to fill the gaps with manual effort. When it works like infrastructure, it becomes the backbone for growth, credibility, and impact.

We’ve helped certification orgs make that leap, from static sites that “do the job” to platforms that do the heavy lifting. The difference isn’t subtle: more leads, smoother workflows, better user experiences, and a team that spends more time advancing the mission and less time patching the tech.

The part that most people miss is that the earlier you make the shift, the more you save. Every patch, rebuild, and workaround you skip means more budget for innovation, better service for your audience, and fewer late nights fixing problems that shouldn’t exist in the first place.

A good site supports your story. A great one helps you live it, and scale it, without losing sleep.

More soon,
Shane

item.title: The four customers you didn't know your certification has
item.description: If you're speaking to everyone, you're probably missing the ones who matter most.
item.content:encoded:
When I ask certification leaders, “Who’s your customer?” I usually get one answer. But here’s the thing, you’ve got at least four.

And if you’re speaking to all of them the same way, you’re leaving trust (and traction) on the table.

Your Four Customers


1️⃣ The Organizations Investing in the Standard
These are the companies paying for the process. They want proof it’s worth the time, money, and internal effort. Your job is to make the business case crystal clear.

2️⃣ The Individuals Earning Credentials
From project managers to technical specialists, they’re on the front lines of compliance. They want tools, clarity, and a clear path to success. (Not a maze of PDFs.)

3️⃣ The Service Providers and Partners
They deliver your standard in the real world. They need training, marketing assets, and ways to prove their expertise so they can win more business.

4️⃣ The Public
The folks who may never read your standard but need to understand why it matters. Public trust drives demand, and demand drives adoption.

The problem is that a single homepage can’t serve all four well.

That’s why the orgs we see growing fastest build a digital ecosystem:

  • Different entry points for different audiences
  • Messaging tailored to their needs
  • Tools and resources designed for each role in the journey

When someone lands on your site, they should see themselves in your story, within seconds. The better you match their goals, the faster they move from “interested” to “invested.” 

And when each audience feels seen, your standard doesn’t just get adopted, it gets championed.

Keep up the good work,
Shane

item.title: Why "more content" isn't the answer
item.description: If your cert org is publishing but still not converting, it's probably not a volume problem.
item.content:encoded:
Let’s be honest, most certification orgs are already creating a good amount of content.

They’ve got blogs, decks, webinars, maybe even a podcast. They’re pushing updates on social, sending emails, sharing resources with partners.

So why does it still feel like… no one’s biting? Why aren’t more people applying, renewing, or sharing what you do?

Here’s what we keep seeing:

It’s not a content problem. It’s a coordination problem.

Content that exists in isolation (even if it’s beautifully written) won’t move the needle. Because most of your audience isn’t reading everything you post. They’re skimming, scrolling, scanning. And unless there’s a clear path forward, they’ll just move on.

When we work with certification teams, we almost always find content that’s good, but scattered.

  • A blog that doesn’t link to the registration.
  • A landing page with no next step.
  • A webinar with no follow-up.
  • Five different teams writing for five different goals.

Instead of content strategy, they’ve accidentally fallen into content drift.

So what’s the fix?

Start with structure.


Not just what you want to say, but where that message fits into the user’s journey.

  • Who is this for?
  • Where are they in the process?
  • And what do they need next?

That’s how your content becomes useful. Not just noise, but navigation. Because in this space, the goal isn’t to flood channels with content.

It’s to create less, and connect more.

And when every piece points to the right next action, that’s when the system starts to work.

Here if you’re trying to make that shift,
Shane

item.title: Is your website pulling its weight?
item.description: If your certification site isn't helping people take action, it's not doing enough.
item.content:encoded:
There’s a pattern I’ve noticed in certification orgs: They treat their website like a brochure, when it should be working more like a control panel.

When you run a certification program, your site isn’t just “marketing.” It’s the place where applicants start their journey, project teams download tools and templates, credential holders check deadlines, partners access brand assets, staff send people for info, etc.

It’s way more than a brochure these days: it’s a critical system.

When we ignore that, we end up with beautiful sites that don’t actually do much and pages that look great, but don’t support the people we serve.

Before you design a page, we recommend starting with these questions:

🔸What actions should this enable?

Can someone start an application without emailing your staff? Can they download what they need without digging through six tabs? 

If not, your site is adding friction, not solving it.

🔸What decisions should it support?

Your users need to know: Is this right for us? Are we eligible? What’s it going to take? 

Your site should answer those questions clearly, without a 30-minute webinar or a PDF maze.

🔸What systems does it need to connect to?

Marketing sites can’t be siloed. They should pull in updates from your standard, link to your certification portal, integrate with your CRM. 

Otherwise, you’re doing double entry. Or worse, leaving gaps in the experience.

When you ask these questions first, the design has a direction. → Form follows function. → Strategy leads the build.

Because in this work, your site shouldn’t just reflect your program, it should help you run it.

If your site isn’t doing what you need it to, it’s not a failure. It just means it was built for a different job. The good news: That’s always fixable.

Onward with purpose,
Shane

item.title: The one thing I tell every certification leader
item.description: If you're managing a program and it feels like no one "gets it," this one's for you.
item.content:encoded:
To kick things off, I want to offer one simple, yet central idea:

Certifications aren’t just about compliance.
They’re one of the most powerful -yet underused- business development tools your clients have.

If you’re scaling or helping a team pursue a certification, and it’s feeling like a burden lately, this post is for you.

Because I’ve seen it happen: the team forgets why we’re taking these additional steps. The story fades. The program starts to stall.

So I want to give you five ways to reframe what a certification really is - and how your clients can use it as a business tool, not just a policy.

1. Structure → it gives them a roadmap.
Big values like sustainability or equity or “healthy workplaces” are great. But they’re also abstract. Certifications take those big ideas and turn them into something their team can act on. Step by step. Credit by credit. They bring shape to the mission.

2. Education → they teach people.
A good framework isn’t just about measuring performance—it’s about building capacity. Helping your client’s team learn what “better” looks like. Whether that’s reducing energy, improving indoor air quality, or making procurement more equitable.

3. Storytelling → they give something to say.
This is the big one. A lot of organizations struggle to talk about what they do in a way that’s specific and credible. But a certification—done right—gives you proof points.
They can say: “We took these steps. Here’s what it means. Here’s why it matters.”

4. Accountability → they hold clients to it.
Third-party review, documentation, recertification—it’s not just red tape. It’s how certifications build trust. Real trust. The kind that your client’s investors, customers, and employees actually pay attention to.

5. Impact → and yeah, they move the needle.
Better performance, better outcomes, better systems. Whether it’s carbon, costs, or credibility, a strong certification makes their business stronger.

I’ve seen orgs forget this. I’ve been in orgs that forget to communicate this.

When the internal story breaks down - when the team forgets the “why” - that’s when things stall. Engagement drops. The standard gets watered down. Marketing gets vague. Product owners get frustrated.

But when the story is strong - when people remember what the certification makes possible? That’s when momentum builds. That’s when the mission clicks. That’s when you start seeing real movement, not just management.

That’s the whole point of this post:
To help you reconnect with what your certification makes possible - so you can run it, grow it, and communicate it with more confidence.

If something I said hit home, or if you’re feeling stuck, reply and let me know.
Seriously. I want to make this newsletter useful, and that starts with hearing from you.

More soon,
Shane
